prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements I find that the case has become stronger, not only more popular. Six members, including colleagues who work in very different areas, independently describe the same two contributions: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which removes Doppler, recoil and first-order light-shift limits while keeping a large number of atoms, and Ye's strontium systems and clock comparisons, which took the scheme to 10^-18. Lindroth, who can judge the atomic physics directly, also confirms that the lattice clock rests on detailed control of polarisabilities and blackbody shifts and is a different step from the frequency comb. Independent confirmation at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE means the result does not depend on one group's claim. My view of the citation is that it should name the invention first and the realisation second, and should not mention the comb, so that the achievement is read as the lattice clock and not as a further prize for spectroscopy. Two names map onto two distinct decisive contributions, which no other shortlisted configuration achieves without an arbitrary cut. I also decline to add a second part. A single, well-supported part is a stronger public position than a pairing in which the second part has one supporter who himself calls its attribution exposed.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not regard them as fully answered. The 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes sit near the clock theme, and a critic can call this a third prize for precision spectroscopy. I accept Kroll's and Mehlig's point that the overlap in people, namely Ye's JILA heritage, must be handled in the citation and cannot simply be asserted away. Two names leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and ion-clock contributors, and the shortlist alone cannot test that fairness. The redefinition of the second has not happened. I regard it as supporting context and not as a condition, because the prize concerns a demonstrated measurement capability, but a reasonable member could wait. For B017, the case against remains that the field is eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unsettled and Cao is outside the credited names. For B003 the case against is timing after the 2025 prize and the unresolved Blais versus Girvin allocation among four names.

responses.point: Olsson asked me directly whether closeness to the 2025 prize is for me a reason to wait on circuit QED or only a presentational issue, and doubts that the 2012 prize is a close precedent for the lattice clock.
responses.response: It is both, and I will say which part carries more weight. Circuit QED, with strong coupling and dispersive readout, is scientifically distinct from macroscopic tunnelling in a circuit, so the presentational problem is the lesser one and could be handled in a citation. The reason to wait is the combination of recency with the credit problem: four names, Blais against Girvin, and no clean way to resolve it within three places. Either alone I could live with, both together I cannot, and this is why I no longer place B003 first. I also agree with her on 2012. Wineland and Haroche rewarded control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock interrogates many neutral atoms with a different idea, so the 2012 prize is a neighbour and not a precedent that closes the topic.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the unsettled pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene does not bear on the merit of the discovery, that the group-leader convention covers the experimental credit, and that a narrow citation on flat bands and correlated states answers my concern about later moire recognition.
responses.response: His distinction between the existence of a tunable correlated platform and the mechanism of its superconductivity is sound, and the comparison with high-temperature superconductivity is fair, since that prize did not wait for a mechanism. That moves me on the scientific question. It does not move me on attribution. The first author of the 2018 papers is outside the credited names, and a convention that credits the group leader is defensible but would be applied to the most visible experiment in a very active field that includes Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov. I would rank B017 as my first alternative and I think it is the most likely next prize in this neighbourhood, but I would want a further year or two of independent reproduction and clearer attribution before putting it ahead of a result as stable as the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll treats the 1989, 2005 and 2012 overlap as a presentational point but not one that can be dismissed entirely, flags his stay in Hall's laboratory for the recusal judgement, and calls the redefinition of the second supporting context only.
responses.response: I agree with his treatment of the precedent and with his view that the redefinition is not a condition. The lattice clock is a separate invention, and the correct response to the overlap is a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 realisation and does not mention frequency combs. On his disclosure, a doctoral stay in Hall's laboratory is a tie to the tradition from which Ye's group comes and not to Ye or Katori, and I would not ask for recusal. I would ask that the record notes it, as he already does. I note that my own disclosure on B003 is a stronger proximity than his on B001, and yet I am prepared to discount my own earlier ranking, so the committee should treat both in the same spirit.

responses.point: Lindroth asks for a frank discussion of whether two names are fair given Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Takamoto and ion-clock contributors, and says that her judgement rests on direct knowledge of polarisabilities and blackbody shifts.
responses.response: I take up the frank discussion she asks for. Katori's concept is a single identifiable proposal, and Ye's group carried it to the record uncertainty and to clock-comparison and many-body clock physics. Ludlow, Hinkley and Takamoto were very important participants, but they worked in the groups of the credited names or on parallel measurements of the same scheme, and Lemonde's group is a further independent confirmation and not the origin of the concept. The three-person limit is also a rule of the prize, and every shortlisted candidate leaves out contributors of this kind. The fair course is to say openly in the public record that the credit is for the concept and for the realisation of the record performance, and that others contributed essential steps. I defer to her on the atomic-physics details, which is the point on which this committee has the most direct expertise.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B027 as a second part to spread the award across fields, but says a clocks-only prize is cleaner and would drop IceCube if colleagues find the single-name attribution unconvincing.
responses.response: I find the attribution unconvincing as he describes it himself, and I would take up his offer to drop it. I do not question the neutrino discovery: the diffuse flux is established. My difficulty is that one name for a collaboration of this size leaves out the early proposers, the detector builders and the analysts, and that the source associations are weaker than the flux. Adding a part chosen to spread the award across fields, and not because it is ready, is not a good reason to add it. A weakly supported second part also risks diluting the clearest candidate on the table. I would keep B027 in view for a later year, perhaps once source identifications are firmer and the committee has considered how to credit a project of this kind, and I say this with respect for his knowledge of the field.

uncertainties: I cannot independently verify the finer history of the magic-wavelength proposal or the exact relative weight of Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy record, because this is outside my own research field and I rely on colleagues with direct knowledge, notably Lindroth.
Whether the committee will treat the 1989, 2005 and 2012 prizes as leaving room for a further precision-measurement award remains a judgement that the ballots alone cannot settle.

Whether the group-leader convention is adequate for the experimental credit in B017, and whether an unsettled pairing mechanism should count against maturity, I leave open, and either answer could change my first alternative within a year or two.
My view on B003 is influenced by subject-matter familiarity in both directions, and I have tried to discount it; Blais versus Girvin cannot be settled within three places.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict with any credited candidate is apparent from my profile. I direct WACQT and work in circuit and waveguide QED, the area of B003 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin), and Chalmers hosted researchers connected with the 2025 prize, so I disclose subject-matter proximity on B003 and defer to the chair on recusal if that candidate is taken up. I no longer prefer B003 and keep it only as a lower alternative. No documented link to Katori, Ye or the other credited names is recorded, and I note Kroll's disclosure on B001 and agree it does not require recusal.
